notes.front: What is the clearance limit in an IFR clearance?
notes.back: The place the clearance authorises flight to: before departure, normally the airport of intended landing.
notes.explanation: Airports and navigation aids often share a name or identifier, so the limit must be understood exactly.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-3, “Clearance Items”
notes.evidence: The traffic clearance issued prior to departure will normally authorize flight to the airport of intended landing. Many airports and associated NAVAIDs are collocated with the same name and/or identifier, so care should be exercised to ensure a clear understanding of the clearance limit.
notes.example: Like the destination on a train ticket, but ATC may write one that stops at a point along the way.

notes.front: What is a “cleared as filed” departure clearance?
notes.back: An abbreviated IFR departure clearance based on the route filed in the flight plan, used when that route needs little or no revision.
notes.explanation: The clearance leans on the filed route, so it only works when ATC can approve that route almost unchanged.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-6, “Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared. . .as Filed) Procedures”
notes.evidence: ATC facilities will issue an abbreviated IFR departure clearance based on the ROUTE of flight filed in the IFR flight plan, provided the filed route can be approved with little or no revision.
notes.example: Like a teacher approving your essay plan “as submitted”, which only works if the plan needs little or no change.

notes.front: What is a clearance void time?
notes.back: A time in a clearance from an airport without a control tower: if the aircraft is not airborne by then, the clearance is void.
notes.explanation: The deadline is part of the clearance itself, so the authority to depart on it runs out at that time.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: A pilot may receive a clearance, when operating from an airport without a control tower, which contains a provision for the clearance to be void if not airborne by a specific time.
notes.example: Like a coupon printed with an expiry time, but on your departure clearance.

notes.front: What does “hold for release” in an IFR clearance mean?
notes.back: You may not depart on that IFR clearance until ATC issues a release time or further instructions.
notes.explanation: ATC uses it to delay a departure for traffic management reasons, such as weather or traffic volume.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: ATC may issue “hold for release” instructions in a clearance to delay an aircraft's departure for traffic management reasons (i.e., weather, traffic volume, etc.). When ATC states in the clearance, “hold for release,” the pilot may not depart utilizing that IFR clearance until a release time or additional instructions are issued by ATC.
notes.example: Like holding a boarding pass but being told to wait at the gate until your row is called.

notes.front: What is a release time?
notes.back: A departure restriction from ATC giving the earliest time an aircraft may depart.
notes.explanation: ATC uses it with traffic management procedures or to separate the departing aircraft from other traffic.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: A “release time” is a departure restriction issued to a pilot by ATC, specifying the earliest time an aircraft may depart. ATC will use “release times” in conjunction with traffic management procedures and/or to separate a departing aircraft from other traffic.
notes.example: Like a shop that opens at nine: you may go in at nine or later, never before.

notes.front: What is pre-taxi clearance?
notes.back: A programme at certain airports letting departing IFR pilots choose to receive their IFR clearance before they start taxiing.
notes.explanation: It exists only at some airports, and the pilot elects whether to take part.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-1, “Pre-taxi Clearance Procedures”
notes.evidence: Certain airports have established pre‐taxi clearance programs whereby pilots of departing instrument flight rules (IFR) aircraft may elect to receive their IFR clearances before they start taxiing for takeoff.
notes.example: Like checking in online before you reach the airport, but for your IFR clearance before you leave the ramp.

notes.front: What is VFR-on-top?
notes.back: An option a pilot on an IFR flight plan in VFR weather may request, choosing their own altitude instead of an assigned one.
notes.explanation: The pilot selects the altitude or flight level, but still subject to any restrictions ATC sets.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: A pilot on an IFR flight plan operating in VFR weather conditions, may request VFR-on-top in lieu of an assigned altitude. This permits a pilot to select an altitude or flight level of their choice (subject to any ATC restrictions.)
notes.example: Like choosing your own seat on a booked flight, but the booking and its rules stay in force.

notes.front: What is an instrument departure procedure (DP)?
notes.back: A preplanned IFR procedure giving obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure.
notes.explanation: It gives a departing aircraft a protected path from the runway until it joins the en route system.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Instrument departure procedures are preplanned instrument flight rule (IFR) procedures which provide obstruction clearance from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure.
notes.example: Like a marked lane out of a busy car park onto the motorway, but drawn to keep you clear of obstacles you cannot see.

notes.front: What is an obstacle departure procedure (ODP)?
notes.back: A DP giving obstruction clearance by the least onerous route from the terminal area to the en route structure.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two types of DP; the other is the standard instrument departure.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: ODPs provide obstruction clearance via the least onerous route from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure.
notes.example: Like the safest footpath down a rocky hillside, but published for pilots who may be climbing through cloud.

notes.front: What is a standard instrument departure (SID)?
notes.back: An ATC procedure, printed graphically, giving obstruction clearance and a transition from the terminal area to the en route structure.
notes.explanation: SIDs are designed mainly for system enhancement and to reduce pilot and controller workload.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Standard Instrument Departures are air traffic control (ATC) procedures printed for pilot/controller use in graphic form to provide obstruction clearance and a transition from the terminal area to the appropriate en route structure. SIDs are primarily designed for system enhancement and to reduce pilot/controller workload.
notes.example: Like a numbered bus route out of the city centre, but for IFR departures and drawn on a chart.

notes.front: What does it mean when a runway passes a diverse departure assessment?
notes.back: An aircraft may turn in any direction from it, within the assessed area, and stay clear of obstacles, so no ODP is published.
notes.explanation: A SID may still be published if ATC needs one.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: If an aircraft may turn in any direction from a runway within the limits of the assessment area (see paragraph 5-2-9e3) and remain clear of obstacles, that runway passes what is called a diverse departure assessment and no ODP will be published. A SID may be published if needed for air traffic control purposes.
notes.example: Like a field with no fences, where you may leave in any direction, but only within the area that was surveyed.

notes.front: What is departure control?
notes.back: An approach control function responsible for ensuring separation between departures.
notes.explanation: To expedite departures it may suggest a takeoff direction other than the one normally used under VFR.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-8, “Departure Control”
notes.evidence: Departure Control is an approach control function responsible for ensuring separation between departures. So as to expedite the handling of departures, Departure Control may suggest a takeoff direction other than that which may normally have been used under VFR handling.
notes.example: Like a steward waving cars out of a stadium car park one by one, but using radar and radio.

notes.front: What are compulsory reporting points?
notes.back: Reporting points on en route charts, shown by a solid triangle, where a position report is required.
notes.explanation: An open triangle marks an “on request” point instead, reported only when ATC asks.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: Reporting points are indicated by symbols on en route charts. The designated compulsory reporting point symbol is a solid triangle and the “on request” reporting point symbol is the open triangle . Reports passing an “on request” reporting point are only necessary when requested by ATC.
notes.example: Like the checkpoints on a rally stage where every crew must call in as it passes.

notes.front: What does a “minimum fuel” advisory tell ATC?
notes.back: Your fuel has reached a state where, on reaching destination, you cannot accept any undue delay.
notes.explanation: It is an advisory only, warning that an emergency could follow if the flight is unduly delayed.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-15, “Minimum Fuel Advisory”
notes.evidence: Advise ATC of your minimum fuel status when your fuel supply has reached a state where, upon reaching destination, you cannot accept any undue delay. Be aware this is not an emergency situation, but merely an advisory that indicates an emergency situation is possible should any undue delay occur.
notes.example: Like telling your host you must leave by ten, without yet asking anyone to drive you home.

notes.front: What is a safety alert from ATC?
notes.back: A controller's warning when aware that an aircraft under their control is at an altitude placing it in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or aircraft.
notes.explanation: The trigger is the controller's own judgment, and it covers only aircraft under that controller's control.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-7, “Safety Alert”
notes.evidence: Issues a safety alert if aware an aircraft under their control is at an altitude which, in the controller's judgment, places the aircraft in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or another aircraft.
notes.example: Like a lifeguard's whistle when a swimmer drifts towards the rocks, but over the radio.

notes.front: Does an ATC clearance authorise a pilot to deviate from a rule, regulation or minimum altitude?
notes.back: No. A clearance authorises flight under specified conditions to prevent collision between known aircraft; it waives no rule.
notes.explanation: A clearance is based only on known traffic and known airport conditions, and serves to prevent collisions between known aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-1, “Clearance”
notes.evidence: A clearance issued by ATC is predicated on known traffic and known physical airport conditions. An ATC clearance means an authorization by ATC, for the purpose of preventing collision between known aircraft, for an aircraft to proceed under specified conditions within controlled airspace. IT IS NOT AUTHORIZATION FOR A PILOT TO DEVIATE FROM ANY RULE, REGULATION, OR MINIMUM ALTITUDE

notes.front: When the clearance limit is the destination airport, what word should follow the airport's name in the clearance?
notes.back: “Airport”.
notes.explanation: Adding the word separates the airport from a navigation aid of the same name or identifier.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-3, “Clearance Items”
notes.evidence: When the clearance limit is the airport of intended landing, the clearance should contain the airport name followed by the word “airport.”

notes.front: Your radios cannot receive the type of signal a clearance requires you to use. What must you do?
notes.back: Notify ATC immediately.
notes.explanation: The FAA makes this the pilot's responsibility, since ATC cannot know what the equipment can receive.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-3, “Clearance Items”
notes.evidence: It is the responsibility of pilots to notify ATC immediately if their radio equipment cannot receive the type of signals they must utilize to comply with their clearance.

notes.front: What does the FAA tell you to do with your clearance when conducting an IFR operation?
notes.back: Make a written record of it.
notes.explanation: The clearance may differ from the flight plan, and ATC may add conditions such as a particular departure route.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: When conducting an IFR operation, make a written record of your clearance. The specified conditions which are a part of your air traffic clearance may be somewhat different from those included in your flight plan. Additionally, ATC may find it necessary to ADD conditions, such as particular departure route.

notes.front: Which parts of clearances and instructions should airborne pilots read back?
notes.back: Those containing altitude assignments, vectors or runway assignments.
notes.explanation: Reading back the numbers is a double check that catches a number misheard or given wrongly.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: Pilots of airborne aircraft should read back those parts of ATC clearances and instructions containing altitude assignments, vectors, or runway assignments as a means of mutual verification. The read back of the “numbers" serves as a double check between pilots and controllers and reduces the kinds of communications errors that occur when a number is either “misheard" or is incorrect.

notes.front: What should every readback and acknowledgement include?
notes.back: The aircraft identification.
notes.explanation: It lets the controller confirm the right aircraft took the instruction, which matters more when the frequency is busy or call signs are similar.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: Include the aircraft identification in all readbacks and acknowledgments. This aids controllers in determining that the correct aircraft received the clearance or instruction. The requirement to include aircraft identification in all readbacks and acknowledgements becomes more important as frequency congestion increases and when aircraft with similar call signs are on the same frequency.

notes.front: A clearance would make you break a regulation or, in your opinion, put the aircraft in jeopardy. Whose responsibility is it to get it changed?
notes.back: Yours: the pilot must request an amended clearance.
notes.explanation: The pilot in command is the final authority for the operation of the aircraft, as § 91.3(a) states.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-1, “Clearance”
notes.evidence: If ATC issues a clearance that would cause a pilot to deviate from a rule or regulation, or in the pilot's opinion, would place the aircraft in jeopardy, IT IS THE PILOT'S RESPONSIBILITY TO REQUEST AN AMENDED CLEARANCE.

notes.front: Under § 91.123(a), what must a pilot who is uncertain of an ATC clearance do?
notes.back: Immediately request clarification from ATC.
notes.explanation: The rule puts the duty on the pilot and makes it immediate.
notes.evidence: When a pilot is uncertain of an ATC clearance, that pilot shall immediately request clarification from ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Once a clearance is obtained, what three situations let a pilot in command deviate from it?
notes.back: An amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists, or the deviation responds to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory.
notes.explanation: Outside these, the clearance binds the pilot in command until it is changed.
notes.evidence: When an ATC clearance has been obtained, no pilot in command may deviate from that clearance unless an amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists, or the deviation is in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under § 91.123(a), where may a pilot not cancel an IFR flight plan even in VFR weather?
notes.back: In Class A airspace.
notes.explanation: Elsewhere the rule lets a pilot cancel IFR when the operation is in VFR weather conditions.
notes.evidence: However, except in Class A airspace, a pilot may cancel an IFR flight plan if the operation is being conducted in VFR weather conditions.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After deviating from a clearance in an emergency, when must the pilot in command notify ATC?
notes.back: As soon as possible.
notes.explanation: The same duty applies after a deviation in response to a collision avoidance resolution advisory.
notes.evidence: Each pilot in command who, in an emergency, or in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory, deviates from an ATC clearance or instruction shall notify ATC of that deviation as soon as possible.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: ATC gives you priority in an emergency but you break no rule. What report may ATC ask for?
notes.back: A detailed report of the emergency to the manager of that ATC facility, within 48 hours, if ATC requests it.
notes.explanation: No rule was broken, yet a report can still be required once ATC has given priority.
notes.evidence: Each pilot in command who (though not deviating from a rule of this subpart) is given priority by ATC in an emergency, shall submit a detailed report of that emergency within 48 hours to the manager of that ATC facility, if requested by ATC.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, how far may the pilot in command deviate from Part 91?
notes.back: From any rule of Part 91, to the extent required to meet that emergency.
notes.explanation: The authority is broad but limited by what the emergency actually requires.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.3(b) (eCFR)
notes.evidence: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: May you fly according to a clearance ATC issued to another aircraft for radar control purposes?
notes.back: No, unless ATC authorises it.
notes.explanation: § 91.123(e) forbids acting on instructions meant for another pilot.
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, no person operating an aircraft may operate that aircraft according to any clearance or instruction that has been issued to the pilot of another aircraft for radar air traffic control purposes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: ATC changes your altitude to maintain and omits altitude restrictions it gave earlier. Do they still apply?
notes.back: No. The last clearance has precedence, and omitted altitude restrictions are cancelled.
notes.explanation: Controllers restate restrictions that still apply, so leaving one out cancels it, even on a departure procedure.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-10, “Adherence to Clearance”
notes.evidence: the last ATC clearance has precedence over the previous ATC clearance. When the route or altitude in a previously issued clearance is amended, the controller will restate applicable altitude restrictions. If altitude to maintain is changed or restated, whether prior to departure or while airborne, and previously issued altitude restrictions are omitted, those altitude restrictions are canceled

notes.front: Does “cleared to (destination) airport as filed” include the en route altitude you filed?
notes.back: No. The altitude is stated in the clearance, or you are told when to expect it.
notes.explanation: The phrase covers the filed route; the altitude comes separately, now or later.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-6, “Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared. . .as Filed) Procedures”
notes.evidence: “Cleared to (destination) airport as filed” does NOT include the en route altitude filed in a flight plan. An en route altitude will be stated in the clearance or the pilot will be advised to expect an assigned or filed altitude within a given time frame or at a certain point after departure.

notes.front: Your filed flight plan was amended after filing. What must you tell ATC in the initial call-up for clearance?
notes.back: That the filed plan has been amended (or replaced), and request a full route clearance.
notes.explanation: The facility issuing the clearance may not yet have received the revised route or plan.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-6, “Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared. . .as Filed) Procedures”
notes.evidence: the responsibility of the pilot to inform ATC in the initial call‐up (for clearance) when the filed flight plan has been either: Amended, or Canceled and replaced with a new filed flight plan. NOTE- The facility issuing a clearance may not have received the revised route or the revised flight plan by the time a pilot requests clearance.

notes.front: What happens if a pilot fails to contact ATC within 30 minutes after the clearance void time?
notes.back: The aircraft is considered overdue and search and rescue procedures begin.
notes.explanation: Other IFR traffic for that airport is held until the pilot calls or the 30 minutes pass.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: Failure of an aircraft to contact ATC within 30 minutes after the clearance void time will result in the aircraft being considered overdue and search and rescue procedures initiated. NOTE- Other IFR traffic for the airport where the clearance is issued is suspended until the aircraft has contacted ATC or until 30 minutes after the clearance void time
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Does an expired clearance void time cancel your IFR flight plan?
notes.back: No. It withdraws your authority to depart IFR until ATC issues a new release and you acknowledge it.
notes.explanation: The flight plan and clearance survive; only the permission to take off under them lapses.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: If the clearance void time expires, it does not cancel the departure clearance or IFR flight plan. It withdraws the pilot's authority to depart IFR until a new departure release/release time has been issued by ATC and is acknowledged by the pilot.

notes.front: A pilot takes off IFR after the clearance void time. What protection is lost?
notes.back: IFR separation. The pilot may also be violating § 91.173, which requires an ATC clearance to operate IFR in controlled airspace.
notes.explanation: After the void time, no valid clearance stands behind the departure.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: Pilots who depart at or after their clearance void time are not afforded IFR separation and may be in violation of 14 CFR section 91.173 which requires that pilots receive an appropriate ATC clearance before operating IFR in controlled airspace.

notes.front: What must ATC issue to a departure from an airport without an operating control tower?
notes.back: Either a departure release (with a release time or void time if applicable) or a hold for release.
notes.explanation: The FAA makes one of the two mandatory for every such departure.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: Departures from an airport without an operating control tower must be issued either a departure release (along with a release time and/or void time if applicable), or a hold for release.

notes.front: Does “hold for release” stop you departing VFR?
notes.back: No. It applies to the IFR clearance; cancel the IFR flight plan and use a VFR code before takeoff.
notes.explanation: An IFR clearance may not be available after departure, so the choice has a cost.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: The ATC instruction, “hold for release,” applies to the IFR clearance and does not prevent the pilot from departing under VFR. However, prior to takeoff the pilot should cancel the IFR flight plan and operate the transponder/ADS-B on the appropriate VFR code. An IFR clearance may not be available after departure.

notes.front: How early do participating pilots call for a pre-taxi clearance?
notes.back: Not more than 10 minutes before proposed taxi time.
notes.explanation: They call clearance delivery or ground control, and get the clearance or delay information on that first call.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-1, “Pre-taxi Clearance Procedures”
notes.evidence: Participating pilots call clearance delivery or ground control not more than 10 minutes before proposed taxi time. IFR clearance (or delay information, if clearance cannot be obtained) is issued at the time of this initial call‐up.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After takeoff, when should you change to the departure control frequency?
notes.back: Not until requested.
notes.explanation: Controllers give the frequency before takeoff, and may omit it if it is published on an assigned DP.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-8, “Departure Control”
notes.evidence: Pilots should not change to the departure control frequency until requested. Controllers may omit the departure control frequency if a DP has or will be assigned and the departure control frequency is published on the DP.

notes.front: May you fly an ODP without an ATC clearance for it?
notes.back: Yes, unless ATC has specifically assigned an alternative departure such as a SID or radar vectors.
notes.explanation: The FAA describes ODPs as recommended for obstruction clearance; the exception is an alternative ATC has assigned.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: ODPs are recommended for obstruction clearance and may be flown without ATC clearance unless an alternate departure procedure (SID or radar vector) has been specifically assigned by ATC.

notes.front: When must you receive an ATC clearance for a SID?
notes.back: Before flying it.
notes.explanation: SIDs are designed mainly for system enhancement and to reduce pilot and controller workload.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: SIDs are primarily designed for system enhancement and to reduce pilot/controller workload. ATC clearance must be received prior to flying a SID.

notes.front: How can you tell a graphic ODP from a SID by its title?
notes.back: A graphic ODP has “(OBSTACLE)” printed in its title.
notes.explanation: Both can be drawn as charts, so the title word is what separates them.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Graphic ODPs will have (OBSTACLE) printed in the procedure title; for example, GEYSR THREE DEPARTURE (OBSTACLE), or, CROWN ONE DEPARTURE (RNAV) (OBSTACLE).

notes.front: What is the primary reason DPs exist?
notes.back: To provide obstacle clearance protection information to pilots.
notes.explanation: A secondary reason, at busier airports, is efficiency and fewer delays through SIDs.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Why are DPs necessary? The primary reason is to provide obstacle clearance protection information to pilots. A secondary reason, at busier airports, is to increase efficiency and reduce communications and departure delays through the use of SIDs.

notes.front: Unless a DP says otherwise, what minimum climb gradient does departure obstacle clearance assume?
notes.back: 200 feet per nautical mile, until the minimum IFR altitude.
notes.explanation: A greater gradient may be published to clear obstacles or meet an ATC crossing restriction.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: maintaining a minimum climb gradient of 200 feet per nautical mile (FPNM), unless required to level off by a crossing restriction, until the minimum IFR altitude. A greater climb gradient may be specified in the DP to clear obstacles or to achieve an ATC crossing restriction.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Departure obstacle clearance assumes you cross the departure end of the runway at what height?
notes.back: At least 35 feet above the elevation of the departure end of the runway.
notes.explanation: The same assumption has you climb to 400 feet above that elevation before the first turn.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: required obstacle clearance for all departures, including diverse, is based on the pilot crossing the departure end of the runway at least 35 feet above the departure end of runway elevation, climbing to 400 feet above the departure end of runway elevation before making the initial turn
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When is a published climb gradient above 200 feet per nautical mile mandatory?
notes.back: When the procedure is part of the ATC clearance, unless increased takeoff minimums are provided and the weather allows them.
notes.explanation: The published higher minimums are the alternative to meeting the steeper gradient.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Compliance with a climb gradient for these purposes is mandatory when the procedure is part of the ATC clearance, unless increased takeoff minimums are provided and weather conditions allow compliance with these minimums.

notes.front: Where can you find a table relating climb gradients to rates of climb at typical groundspeeds?
notes.back: In the front matter of every Terminal Procedures Publication booklet.
notes.explanation: The table pairs each gradient with typical groundspeeds, since the same gradient needs a different rate of climb at each speed.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 1, “Departure Procedures”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: relates specific climb gradients and typical groundspeeds.

notes.front: To which operators does § 91.175(f), civil airport takeoff minimums, apply?
notes.back: Those operating under Part 121, 125, 129 or 135.
notes.explanation: The paragraph names those four parts only, so it does not bind a Part 91 operator.
notes.evidence: (f) Civil airport takeoff minimums. This paragraph applies to persons operating an aircraft under part 121, 125, 129, or 135 of this chapter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Where no takeoff minimums are prescribed, what visibility does § 91.175(f) require for an aeroplane with two engines or fewer?
notes.back: 1 statute mile.
notes.explanation: Aircraft with more than two engines need only half a statute mile.
notes.evidence: (i) For aircraft, other than helicopters, having two engines or less—1 statute mile visibility. (ii) For aircraft having more than two engines— 1/2 statute mile visibility.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Departing IFR under Part 91, not filed or cleared for an ODP, SID or diverse vector area headings, who is responsible for obstacle clearance?
notes.back: The pilot.
notes.explanation: DPs are built so that flying their path and climb ensures obstacle protection; without one, that protection is the pilot's to provide.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: DPs are designed so that the pilot's adherence to the procedure's lateral path and vertical climb requirements will ensure obstacle protection. Obstacle clearance responsibility rests with the pilot when he/she chooses to depart IFR under 14 CFR part 91 and has not filed or been cleared for an ODP or an ATC-assigned SID or assigned headings for a DVA

notes.front: You are established on a SID and ATC vectors you off it. What happens to the SID?
notes.back: Consider it cancelled, unless the controller adds “expect to resume SID”.
notes.explanation: Be ready to rejoin the SID at a later fix or leg if the controller says to expect to resume it.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: After an aircraft is established on a SID and subsequently vectored or cleared to deviate off of the SID or SID transition, pilots must consider the SID canceled, unless the controller adds “expect to resume SID;” pilots should then be prepared to rejoin the SID at a subsequent fix or procedure leg.

notes.front: ATC vectors you off an ODP. Who takes responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance?
notes.back: ATC. The ODP is cancelled at that point.
notes.explanation: Even then, the minimum climb gradient of 200 feet per nautical mile is assumed.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Aircraft may be vectored off of an ODP, or issued an altitude lower than a published altitude on an ODP, at which time the ODP is canceled. In these cases, ATC assumes responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance. In all cases, the minimum 200 FPNM climb gradient is assumed.

notes.front: Under § 91.183, what must the pilot in command of an IFR flight in controlled airspace maintain on the radio?
notes.back: A continuous watch on the appropriate frequency.
notes.explanation: The same rule then lists the reports the pilot must make as soon as possible.
notes.evidence: Unless otherwise authorized by ATC, the pilot in command of each aircraft operated under IFR in controlled airspace must ensure that a continuous watch is maintained on the appropriate frequency
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Under § 91.183, what weather must an IFR pilot report as soon as possible?
notes.back: Any unforecast weather conditions encountered.
notes.explanation: The rule also requires reports of any other information relating to the safety of flight.
notes.evidence: (b) Any unforecast weather conditions encountered; and (c) Any other information relating to the safety of flight.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On airways, does a flight cleared “VFR-on-top” still report over compulsory reporting points?
notes.back: Yes. All flights, at any altitude, report over each designated compulsory reporting point on the route.
notes.explanation: The FAA names VFR-on-top flights explicitly in this requirement.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: A position report is required by all flights regardless of altitude, including those operating in accordance with an ATC clearance specifying “VFR-on-top,” over each designated compulsory reporting point along the route being flown.

notes.front: After ATC says “radar contact”, what happens to position reports, and what makes you start again?
notes.back: Stop reporting over designated points; resume when ATC says “radar contact lost” or “radar service terminated”.
notes.explanation: “Radar contact” is the cue to stop; the FAA gives the two phrases that end it.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: When informed by ATC that their aircraft are in “Radar Contact,” pilots should discontinue position reports over designated reporting points. They should resume normal position reporting when ATC advises “RADAR CONTACT LOST” or “RADAR SERVICE TERMINATED.”

notes.front: Which position report item may be left out of IFR reports made directly to Centre or approach control?
notes.back: The type of flight plan.
notes.explanation: Every other item on the FAA list still goes in the report.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: Type of flight plan (not required in IFR position reports made directly to ARTCCs or approach control)

notes.front: In a position report, what do you give for the next reporting point, and for the one after it?
notes.back: The estimated time and name of the next point; only the name of the one after.
notes.explanation: The report looks two points ahead: a time for the next, a name only for the one after.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: ETA and name of next reporting point; The name only of the next succeeding reporting point along the route of flight; and Pertinent remarks.

notes.front: Without being asked, when must you report leaving an altitude?
notes.back: When vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level for a newly assigned one.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the reports the FAA says to make at all times without a specific ATC request.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-3, “Additional Reports”
notes.evidence: The following reports should be made to ATC or FSS facilities without a specific ATC request: At all times. When vacating any previously assigned altitude or flight level for a newly assigned altitude or flight level.

notes.front: What change in cruising true airspeed must you report to ATC without being asked?
notes.back: A change of 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from the filed airspeed.
notes.explanation: The same threshold appears in the FAA's list of pilot duties for speed.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-3, “Additional Reports”
notes.evidence: Change in the average true airspeed (at cruising altitude) when it varies by 5 percent or 10 knots (whichever is greater) from that filed in the flight plan.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Within what tolerance should you hold a speed assigned by ATC?
notes.back: Plus or minus 10 knots, or 0.02 Mach, of the specified speed.
notes.explanation: The tolerance applies to published and assigned speeds alike.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-12, “Speed Adjustments”
notes.evidence: Pilots complying with speed adjustments (published or assigned) are expected to maintain a speed within plus or minus 10 knots or 0.02 Mach number of the specified speed.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does the controller give first priority to?
notes.back: Separation of aircraft and the issuing of radar safety alerts.
notes.explanation: Other required services come second, and additional services third, as far as possible.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-1, “General”
notes.evidence: The air traffic controller is responsible to give first priority to the separation of aircraft and to the issuance of radar safety alerts, second priority to other services that are required, but do not involve separation of aircraft and third priority to additional services to the extent possible.

notes.front: Why do pilot and controller responsibilities overlap in many areas?
notes.back: To give redundancy: if one party fails, the other's overlapping responsibility is expected to compensate.
notes.explanation: The overlap is intentional, not an accident of the rules.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-1, “General”
notes.evidence: The responsibilities of the pilot and the controller intentionally overlap in many areas providing a degree of redundancy. Should one or the other fail in any manner, this overlapping responsibility is expected to compensate, in many cases, for failures that may affect safety.

notes.front: Between which flights do IFR traffic clearances provide standard separation?
notes.back: Only between IFR flights.
notes.explanation: VFR flights may be operating in the same area without ATC's knowledge, so avoiding them in good weather is the pilot's job.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-1, “Clearance”
notes.evidence: When weather conditions permit, during the time an IFR flight is operating, it is the direct responsibility of the pilot to avoid other aircraft since VFR flights may be operating in the same area without the knowledge of ATC. Traffic clearances provide standard separation only between IFR flights.

notes.front: What are the two types of safety alert?
notes.back: A terrain or obstruction alert, and an aircraft conflict alert.
notes.explanation: With a conflict alert, the controller also offers an alternative if feasible.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-7, “Safety Alert”
notes.evidence: Types of safety alerts are: Terrain or Obstruction Alert.Immediately issued to an aircraft under their control if aware the aircraft is at an altitude believed to place the aircraft in unsafe proximity to terrain or obstructions. Aircraft Conflict Alert.

notes.front: Does a minimum fuel advisory get you traffic priority?
notes.back: No. It does not imply a need for traffic priority.
notes.explanation: If you need priority to land safely, the FAA says to declare an emergency instead.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-15, “Minimum Fuel Advisory”
notes.evidence: Be aware a minimum fuel advisory does not imply a need for traffic priority. If the remaining usable fuel supply suggests the need for traffic priority to ensure a safe landing, you should declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes.

notes.front: On initial contact, where in your call should the words “minimum fuel” come?
notes.back: Right after your call sign.
notes.explanation: The term goes on initial contact, not later in the exchange.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-15, “Minimum Fuel Advisory”
notes.evidence: On initial contact the term “minimum fuel” should be used after stating call sign.

notes.front: On a “maintain VFR-on-top” clearance, what altitude must you fly?
notes.back: The appropriate VFR cruising altitude under § 91.159.
notes.explanation: You must also meet VFR visibility and cloud clearance, and the IFR rules that apply to the flight.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: When operating in VFR conditions with an ATC authorization to “maintain VFR-on-top/maintain VFR conditions” pilots on IFR flight plans must: Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude as prescribed in 14 CFR section 91.159. Comply with the VFR visibility and distance from cloud criteria in 14 CFR section 91.155 (Basic VFR Weather Minimums).

notes.front: On a VFR-on-top clearance, which IFR rules still apply?
notes.back: Those applicable to the flight, such as minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, radio communications and adherence to clearance.
notes.explanation: These apply alongside the VFR altitude and weather minimums the clearance also requires.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: Comply with instrument flight rules that are applicable to this flight; i.e., minimum IFR altitudes, position reporting, radio communications, course to be flown, adherence to ATC clearance, etc.

notes.front: Does a VFR-on-top clearance cancel your IFR flight plan?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The FAA calls it imperative that pilots understand this.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: It is imperative, however, that pilots understand that clearance to operate “VFR-on-top/VFR conditions” does not imply cancellation of the IFR flight plan.

notes.front: In which airspace will ATC not authorise VFR-on-top?
notes.back: Class A airspace.
notes.explanation: The FAA states the ban directly and refers to its Class A airspace paragraph.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top operations in Class A airspace.

notes.front: Outside Class B airspace and TRSAs, does ATC separate you from other aircraft while you fly VFR-on-top?
notes.back: No. ATC may issue traffic advisories, but seeing and avoiding other aircraft is solely your responsibility.
notes.explanation: IFR separation is provided to all IFR flight plans except during that VFR-on-top part of the flight.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-11, “IFR Separation Standards”
notes.evidence: except during that part of the flight (outside Class B airspace or a TRSA) being conducted on a VFR-on-top/VFR conditions clearance. Under these conditions, ATC may issue traffic advisories, but it is the sole responsibility of the pilot to be vigilant so as to see and avoid other aircraft.

notes.front: In the FAA's clearance shorthand, what does `CAF RH RV V18 40` mean?
notes.back: Cleared as filed, maintain runway heading for radar vector to Victor 18, climb to 4,000.
notes.explanation: Altitudes are written in hundreds of feet, so 40 stands for 4,000.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-15B, 2012), appendix A, “Clearance Shorthand”, p. A-1
notes.evidence: Example: CAF RH RV V18 40 SQ 0700 DPC 120.4 Cleared as filed, maintain runway heading for radar vector

notes.front: Your clearance reads “cleared to the Ridgeway VOR”, and a Ridgeway airport lies beside it. What have you been cleared to?
notes.back: The Ridgeway VOR, not the airport.
notes.explanation: A limit that is the airport should carry the word “airport”; one that is a known navigation aid should state its type.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-3, “Clearance Items”
notes.evidence: When the clearance limit is the airport of intended landing, the clearance should contain the airport name followed by the word “airport.” Under certain conditions, a clearance limit may be a NAVAID or other fix. When the clearance limit is a NAVAID, intersection, or waypoint and the type is known, the clearance should contain type.
notes.choices:
A) The Ridgeway VOR
B) Ridgeway airport
C) Whichever is nearer your route
D) Your filed destination
notes.choicesExplained: B would have been named with the word “airport”. C: the limit is fixed by the clearance, not by your route. D: the clearance limit replaces the filed destination as the point you may fly to.

notes.front: ATC tells you: “Turn left heading 240, descend and maintain 5,000.” What should you read back?
notes.back: The heading and the altitude, with your aircraft identification.
notes.explanation: Altitude assignments and vectors are the numbers to read back, and every readback carries the aircraft identification.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: Pilots of airborne aircraft should read back those parts of ATC clearances and instructions containing altitude assignments, vectors, or runway assignments as a means of mutual verification.
notes.choices:
A) “Roger”
B) The heading and altitude, with your identification
C) Only the altitude
D) Your call sign alone
notes.choicesExplained: A and D acknowledge without verifying the numbers. C leaves out the vector, which is also read back.

notes.front: In cloud, ATC clears you to descend to an altitude you know is below the published minimum for your route. What should you do?
notes.back: Request an amended clearance rather than descend.
notes.explanation: A clearance never authorises flight below a minimum altitude, and the pilot must ask for a change.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-1, “Clearance”
notes.evidence: If ATC issues a clearance that would cause a pilot to deviate from a rule or regulation, or in the pilot's opinion, would place the aircraft in jeopardy, IT IS THE PILOT'S RESPONSIBILITY TO REQUEST AN AMENDED CLEARANCE.
notes.choices:
A) Descend; ATC is responsible
B) Request an amended clearance
C) Descend and report later
D) Cancel IFR at once
notes.choicesExplained: A and C assume the clearance covers the rule, which it never does. D is not possible in cloud and does not fix the problem.

notes.front: Clearance delivery says: “cleared to Millbrook airport as filed.” You filed 8,000 feet. What altitude are you cleared to?
notes.back: None yet from that phrase: expect ATC to state an altitude, or when to expect one.
notes.explanation: “As filed” covers the filed route, not the filed en route altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-6, “Abbreviated IFR Departure Clearance (Cleared. . .as Filed) Procedures”
notes.evidence: “Cleared to (destination) airport as filed” does NOT include the en route altitude filed in a flight plan.
notes.choices:
A) 8,000 feet
B) None yet; ATC will state an altitude or when to expect it
C) The minimum IFR altitude
D) Any altitude you choose
notes.choicesExplained: A is the common mistake: the filed altitude is not included. C and D have no basis in the clearance.

notes.front: At a non-towered field your clearance is void if not off by 1430. A passenger delay means you are still on the ground at 1432. What now?
notes.back: Do not depart IFR; advise ATC of your intentions as soon as possible.
notes.explanation: The void time has withdrawn your authority to depart IFR until ATC issues a new release.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: A pilot who does not depart prior to the clearance void time must advise ATC as soon as possible of their intentions.
notes.choices:
A) Depart at once on the same clearance
B) Advise ATC of your intentions as soon as possible
C) Wait 30 minutes, then depart
D) Depart VFR on the IFR transponder code
notes.choicesExplained: A: after the void time you get no IFR separation. C: 30 minutes is the most time ATC allows for your call, not a waiting period. D: going VFR means first cancelling the IFR flight plan and using a VFR code, and ATC still needs to hear your intentions.

notes.front: You are told “hold for release, expect 20 minutes departure delay.” The weather is good VFR and you want to go now. What does the FAA allow?
notes.back: Cancel the IFR flight plan, squawk a VFR code and depart VFR.
notes.explanation: Hold for release applies only to the IFR clearance; you accept that an IFR clearance may not be available later.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: The ATC instruction, “hold for release,” applies to the IFR clearance and does not prevent the pilot from departing under VFR. However, prior to takeoff the pilot should cancel the IFR flight plan
notes.choices:
A) Depart IFR and call ATC once airborne
B) Cancel IFR and depart VFR on a VFR code
C) Depart VFR keeping the IFR plan open
D) Nothing; you must wait
notes.choicesExplained: A: you may not depart on the IFR clearance until released. C: the IFR plan should be cancelled before a VFR takeoff. D: a VFR departure remains open to you.

notes.front: Which of these lets you deviate from your clearance without an amended one?
notes.back: An emergency.
notes.explanation: Apart from an amended clearance, § 91.123(a) allows only an emergency or a collision avoidance resolution advisory.
notes.evidence: no pilot in command may deviate from that clearance unless an amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists, or the deviation is in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory.
notes.choices:
A) Light turbulence at your altitude
B) A shorter route you would prefer
C) An emergency
D) A traffic advisory on your display
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are reasons to request an amendment, not to deviate. D: a traffic advisory alone never justifies deviating.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: An electrical fire fills the cabin with smoke and you must land at once, which means breaking a Part 91 rule. How far may you deviate?
notes.back: As far as needed to meet the emergency.
notes.explanation: § 91.3(b) lets the pilot in command deviate from any Part 91 rule, but only to the extent required.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.3(b) (eCFR)
notes.evidence: the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of this part to the extent required to meet that emergency.
notes.choices:
A) Not at all without ATC approval
B) As far as needed to meet the emergency
C) From any rule, for the rest of the flight
D) Only from altitude rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: the authority does not wait for ATC. C goes beyond what the emergency requires. D: the rule covers any Part 91 rule.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a VFR-on-top clearance you are flying a magnetic course of 090°, above 3,000 feet AGL. Which altitude fits the rules?
notes.back: 5,500 feet, a VFR cruising altitude (odd thousands plus 500 for this course).
notes.explanation: VFR-on-top requires the VFR cruising altitude of § 91.159, not an IFR one.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: Fly at the appropriate VFR altitude as prescribed in 14 CFR section 91.159.
notes.choices:
A) 5,000 feet
B) 5,500 feet
C) 6,000 feet
D) 6,500 feet
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are IFR-style thousands, not VFR cruising altitudes. D is a VFR altitude for westerly courses.

notes.front: You are cruising at FL 200 on an IFR flight plan above a solid deck and ask for VFR-on-top. What should you expect?
notes.back: ATC will not authorise it, because FL 200 is in Class A airspace.
notes.explanation: VFR and VFR-on-top operations are not authorised in Class A airspace.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-8, “IFR Clearance VFR-on-top”
notes.evidence: ATC will not authorize VFR or VFR-on-top operations in Class A airspace.
notes.choices:
A) Approval, subject to traffic
B) Refusal: Class A airspace
C) Approval above FL 180 only with a top report
D) Approval if you cancel IFR
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the Class A ban. D: IFR cannot be cancelled in Class A either.

notes.front: At a non-towered airport your IFR clearance mentions no departure procedure, but the runway has a textual ODP. May you fly it?
notes.back: Yes. ODPs may be flown without ATC clearance unless ATC assigns another departure.
notes.explanation: ODPs exist for obstruction clearance and do not need ATC approval.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: ODPs are recommended for obstruction clearance and may be flown without ATC clearance unless an alternate departure procedure (SID or radar vector) has been specifically assigned by ATC.
notes.choices:
A) No, it must be in your clearance
B) Yes, unless ATC assigned another departure
C) Only in VFR conditions
D) Only if you filed it
notes.choicesExplained: A and D treat the ODP like a SID, which does need a clearance. C: nothing in the FAA limits ODPs to VFR conditions.

notes.front: Your clearance includes a DP requiring 350 feet per nautical mile to 3,000 feet. Your aircraft manages only 250 on this hot day. What follows?
notes.back: You cannot accept it as cleared, unless published higher takeoff minimums exist and the weather meets them.
notes.explanation: A gradient in a procedure that is part of your clearance is mandatory, so a shortfall needs another option.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: Compliance with a climb gradient for these purposes is mandatory when the procedure is part of the ATC clearance, unless increased takeoff minimums are provided and weather conditions allow compliance with these minimums.
notes.choices:
A) Fly it; gradients are advisory
B) You cannot comply as cleared, unless higher minimums apply and are met
C) Climb at 250 and turn early
D) Climb at 200, the standard
notes.choicesExplained: A: the gradient is mandatory when the procedure is in your clearance. C and D fall short of the published gradient.

notes.front: A DP needs 200 feet per nautical mile, and your climb groundspeed is 120 knots (2 nautical miles a minute). What rate of climb meets it?
notes.back: About 400 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: Covering 2 nautical miles each minute at 200 feet per mile means 400 feet each minute; the rate of climb table does this sum for you.
notes.source: FAA, Instrument Procedures Handbook (FAA-H-8083-16B), ch. 1, “Departure Procedures”, p. 1-17
notes.evidence: relates specific climb gradients and typical groundspeeds.
notes.choices:
A) 200 feet per minute
B) 400 feet per minute
C) 600 feet per minute
D) 800 feet per minute
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores groundspeed. C would suit 180 knots. D would suit 240 knots.

notes.front: A Part 91 pilot plans an IFR takeoff with visibility below the published takeoff minimums. Does § 91.175(f) forbid it?
notes.back: No. That paragraph applies to Part 121, 125, 129 and 135 operators.
notes.explanation: The paragraph names only those four parts of the regulations.
notes.evidence: This paragraph applies to persons operating an aircraft under part 121, 125, 129, or 135 of this chapter.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, always
B) No; it applies to Parts 121, 125, 129 and 135
C) Yes, unless the aircraft is single-engine
D) Only at towered airports
notes.choicesExplained: A and C misread who the paragraph covers. D: towers have nothing to do with it.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A controller issues you a vector towards rising terrain that you believe is wrong. What do the pilot and controller roles expect of you?
notes.back: Question the heading; both of you share the safety duty.
notes.explanation: Pilot and controller duties overlap on purpose, so each can catch the other's mistake.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-6, “Vectors”
notes.evidence: Questions any assigned heading or altitude believed to be incorrect.
notes.choices:
A) Fly it; the controller is responsible
B) Question the heading
C) Ignore it and fly your own heading
D) Cancel IFR
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the redundancy unused. C deviates from an instruction without an emergency. D does not solve the problem.

notes.front: On an IFR flight in radar contact, in clear weather, you spot a light aircraft ahead at your level that ATC has not called. Whose job is it to avoid it?
notes.back: Yours.
notes.explanation: In weather that permits, the pilot must see and avoid, whatever the flight plan or radar service.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-8, “See and Avoid”
notes.evidence: When meteorological conditions permit, regardless of type of flight plan or whether or not under control of a radar facility, the pilot is responsible to see and avoid other traffic
notes.choices:
A) ATC's, because you are IFR
B) Yours
C) The other pilot's only
D) Nobody's until ATC issues a traffic call
notes.choicesExplained: A and D assume ATC separates you from VFR traffic, which it does not. C: seeing and avoiding is every pilot's duty.

notes.front: In cloud on an IFR flight, you plan to switch your only radio to a weather broadcast for five minutes without telling ATC. What rule does this breach?
notes.back: The duty to keep a continuous watch on the appropriate frequency, § 91.183.
notes.explanation: Unless ATC authorises otherwise, the IFR pilot in command must keep that watch.
notes.evidence: the pilot in command of each aircraft operated under IFR in controlled airspace must ensure that a continuous watch is maintained on the appropriate frequency
notes.choices:
A) None, if the transponder is on
B) The continuous watch requirement
C) The readback rule
D) Only a VFR rule
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule asks for a listening watch, which a transponder is not. C concerns clearances you receive. D: this is an IFR rule.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Instrument Rating ACS and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On an airway, not in radar contact, you pass a solid triangle on the chart. What do you do?
notes.back: Make a position report.
notes.explanation: A solid triangle is a compulsory reporting point; an open triangle would need a report only on request.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: The designated compulsory reporting point symbol is a solid triangle
notes.choices:
A) Report position
B) Report only if ATC asks
C) Nothing; reports are for VFR flights
D) Change to the next frequency
notes.choicesExplained: B describes an open triangle. C: IFR flights report at compulsory points. D: the symbol concerns reporting, not frequencies.

notes.front: Which item belongs in a non-radar IFR position report to Centre?
notes.back: The estimated time over the next reporting point.
notes.explanation: The type of flight plan may be omitted in reports to Centre, and remarks are included only when pertinent.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-2, “Position Reporting”
notes.evidence: ETA and name of next reporting point; The name only of the next succeeding reporting point along the route of flight
notes.choices:
A) Your departure time
B) The estimated time at the next reporting point
C) Your fuel on board
D) Your destination weather
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are not among the items the FAA lists for a position report.

notes.front: In icing, your aircraft can climb only at 300 feet per minute towards a newly assigned altitude. What should you do?
notes.back: Tell ATC, without waiting to be asked.
notes.explanation: Being unable to climb at least 500 feet per minute is one of the reports made without an ATC request.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-3-3, “Additional Reports”
notes.evidence: When unable to climb/descend at a rate of a least 500 feet per minute.
notes.choices:
A) Report it to ATC now
B) Say nothing until ATC asks
C) Level off and wait
D) Report after reaching altitude
notes.choicesExplained: B and D delay a report ATC needs now. C would also need a report, and does not reach the assigned altitude.

notes.front: Nearing your destination you realise any undue delay would leave you short, but you do not yet need priority. What do you say?
notes.back: “Minimum fuel”, after your call sign on initial contact.
notes.explanation: The advisory warns of a possible emergency without asking for priority.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-15, “Minimum Fuel Advisory”
notes.evidence: Advise ATC of your minimum fuel status when your fuel supply has reached a state where, upon reaching destination, you cannot accept any undue delay.
notes.choices:
A) MAYDAY
B) PAN-PAN
C) “Minimum fuel”
D) Nothing yet
notes.choicesExplained: A and B declare emergencies you do not yet have. D leaves ATC unaware of a state it should plan around.

notes.front: What are two differences between an ODP and a SID?
notes.back: An ODP may be flown without ATC clearance and may be textual; a SID needs clearance and is always graphic.
notes.explanation: ODPs exist for obstruction clearance, while SIDs are ATC procedures designed mainly for system efficiency.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-9, “Instrument Departure Procedures (DP)”
notes.evidence: There are two types of DPs, Obstacle Departure Procedures (ODP), printed either textually or graphically, and Standard Instrument Departures (SID), always printed graphically.

notes.front: How does a clearance void time differ from a release time?
notes.back: A void time is the latest you may be airborne on the clearance; a release time is the earliest you may depart.
notes.explanation: One closes the departure window and the other opens it.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-2-7, “Departure Restrictions, Clearance Void Times, Hold for Release, and Release Times”
notes.evidence: A “release time” is a departure restriction issued to a pilot by ATC, specifying the earliest time an aircraft may depart.

notes.front: When should you declare an emergency for low fuel rather than report “minimum fuel”?
notes.back: When your remaining fuel suggests you need traffic priority to land safely.
notes.explanation: Minimum fuel is only an advisory and brings no priority; an emergency does.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 5-5-15, “Minimum Fuel Advisory”
notes.evidence: If the remaining usable fuel supply suggests the need for traffic priority to ensure a safe landing, you should declare an emergency due to low fuel and report fuel remaining in minutes.

notes.front: How should you respond differently to a collision avoidance resolution advisory than to a traffic advisory?
notes.back: Respond at once and manoeuvre as the resolution advisory shows; a traffic advisory alone never justifies deviating.
notes.explanation: Only the resolution advisory recommends vertical manoeuvres; afterwards, notify ATC as soon as practicable.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-16, “Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS I & II)”
notes.evidence: When an RA occurs, pilots should respond immediately to the RA displays and maneuver as indicated unless doing so would jeopardize the safe operation of the flight
